tests.title: Unit 1: Introduction to Economics – Practice Test 1

questions.question_text: Who is regarded as the Father of Economics, and which book did he write?
options: Adam Smith – The Wealth of Nations
Lionel Robbins – Nature and Significance of Economic Science
questions.explanation: Adam Smith wrote An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations (1776).

questions.question_text: The word "economics" comes from the Greek words oikos and nomos, which literally mean:
questions.explanation: Oikos means household and nomos means management or rules, so literally "household management".

questions.question_text: Adam Smith's wealth definition treats economics as the study of:
questions.explanation: Smith defined economics as an inquiry into the nature and causes of the wealth of nations.

questions.question_text: Which is a criticism of the wealth definition?
options: It gives too much importance to wealth and neglects human welfare
It treats economics as a normative science only
It ignores the role of production
questions.explanation: Critics said it made wealth the end and man the means, neglecting human welfare.

questions.question_text: Carlyle called economics the "dismal science" mainly because:
options: It could not be tested by experiments
It was seen as focusing on selfish wealth-getting while ignoring human welfare
questions.explanation: The wealth definition made economics seem cold and materialistic, so Carlyle called it dismal.

questions.question_text: Marshall defined economics as a study of mankind in the ordinary business of life that examines:
options: Only scarce means with alternative uses
How individuals and society use material requisites of well-being
questions.explanation: Marshall's welfare definition links economics to the attainment of material welfare.

questions.question_text: Which is a main feature of Marshall's welfare definition?
options: It considers non-material welfare as central
It makes man the centre and wealth only a means to welfare
questions.explanation: Marshall stressed that wealth is a means to human welfare, not an end.

questions.question_text: Which is a criticism of Marshall's definition?
options: It restricts economics to material welfare and ignores services
questions.explanation: Critics said it wrongly excluded non-material welfare such as the services of doctors and teachers.

questions.question_text: The distinction between material and non-material welfare is considered artificial because:
options: Welfare is a unified feeling and cannot be split clearly
questions.explanation: Both kinds of goods contribute to one overall satisfaction, so the split is arbitrary.

questions.question_text: Robbins defined economics as the science that studies human behaviour as a relationship between:
options: Ends and scarce means which have alternative uses
questions.explanation: This is the scarcity definition from An Essay on the Nature and Significance of Economic Science (1932).

questions.question_text: Which is NOT an element of Robbins' definition?
questions.explanation: Robbins' elements are unlimited ends, scarce means, alternative uses and the need to choose.

questions.question_text: "Economics is neutral between ends" means economics:
options: Studies only means and not the morality of ends
Judges whether ends are good or bad
questions.explanation: Economics does not say whether wants are desirable; it only studies how scarce means are allocated.

questions.question_text: Which is a criticism of Robbins' definition?
options: It ignores economic growth and development
questions.explanation: The definition is static and does not deal with growth, employment or development.

questions.question_text: Robbins' definition makes economics a purely positive science because it:
options: Is silent on what ought to be and only explains what is
questions.explanation: By staying neutral between ends, it avoids value judgements.

questions.question_text: Samuelson's growth definition emphasises:
options: Choice over time with scarce resources to produce goods and distribute them for growth
questions.explanation: It adds the dynamic element of time and economic growth to the scarcity idea.

questions.question_text: Samuelson's definition improves on Robbins' by:
options: Adding the dynamic dimension of growth and time
questions.explanation: It covers growth and dynamic problems, which the static scarcity definition left out.

questions.question_text: Which pairing of definition and economist is correct?
questions.explanation: Wealth: Smith; Welfare: Marshall; Scarcity: Robbins; Growth: Samuelson.

questions.question_text: Which definition is the most widely accepted today?
questions.explanation: Robbins' scarcity definition is the most widely accepted because it is analytical and universal.

questions.question_text: Scarcity differs from shortage because scarcity:
options: Is a universal condition of limited resources relative to wants, while shortage is a temporary supply gap at a price
questions.explanation: Scarcity exists for all resources always; shortage is a temporary market imbalance.

questions.question_text: The basic economic problem arises from:
questions.explanation: Wants are endless but resources are limited, forcing choice.

questions.question_text: Which is a characteristic of human wants?
options: They cannot be influenced by advertising
questions.explanation: Wants are unlimited, recur, differ in intensity and can be satisfied in part.

questions.question_text: "Alternative uses of resources" means resources:
options: Can be used in more than one way
questions.explanation: Land, labour and capital can produce different goods, so using them for one forgoes another.

questions.question_text: The scope of economics includes:
options: Both the subject matter and the nature (science/art, positive/normative)
questions.explanation: Scope covers what economics studies and what kind of discipline it is.

questions.question_text: The subject matter of economics is:
options: How individuals, firms and society make choices about scarce resources
questions.explanation: It deals with consumption, production, exchange and distribution of scarce resources.

questions.question_text: Which is NOT a traditional division of economics?
questions.explanation: The four divisions are consumption, production, exchange and distribution.

tests.title: Unit 1: Introduction to Economics – Practice Test 2

questions.question_text: Economics is called a science because it:
options: Systematically studies cause-and-effect relationships and formulates laws
questions.explanation: It collects facts, analyses them and formulates generalisations, though its laws are less exact.

questions.question_text: Economics is also called an art because it:
options: Gives practical guidance for solving economic problems
questions.explanation: Art means applying knowledge for practical ends, such as policy making.

questions.question_text: Economic laws are called tendencies because:
options: They hold exactly in every case
They hold only on average or under given conditions, as human behaviour varies
questions.explanation: Human behaviour is not uniform, so laws state what generally tends to happen.

questions.question_text: "Ceteris paribus" means:
questions.explanation: It isolates the effect of one variable by holding others constant.

questions.question_text: Controlled experimentation is difficult in economics because:
options: Human behaviour and social conditions cannot be controlled like laboratory conditions
questions.explanation: Economic agents are people and conditions keep changing.

questions.question_text: The relationship between economics and political science is close because:
options: Government policies on taxes, spending and regulation depend on both
questions.explanation: Policy decisions combine political choices with economic analysis.

questions.question_text: Economics is related to sociology because:
options: Social customs and class structure affect consumption and savings
Society has no effect on markets
questions.explanation: Social norms, habits and institutions influence economic behaviour.

questions.question_text: Mathematics and statistics help economics by:
options: Providing tools to build models, measure and test relationships
questions.explanation: Equations, graphs and data analysis give precision to economic analysis.

questions.question_text: Economics is related to psychology because:
options: Wants are unrelated to the mind
Consumer tastes, motives and expectations influence economic decisions
questions.explanation: Understanding behaviour is central to demand analysis.

questions.question_text: Which is a reason for studying economics?
options: It helps in rational decision making about scarce resources
It eliminates the need for government
questions.explanation: Economics trains one to weigh costs and benefits and understand the economy.

questions.question_text: Economics helps consumers mainly by:
options: Guiding them to spend income to get maximum satisfaction
questions.explanation: Consumer theory shows how to allocate income across goods.

questions.question_text: Economics helps producers by:
options: Helping them decide what, how and how much to produce at least cost
Telling them which goods to ban
questions.explanation: Cost, demand and market analysis guide production decisions.

questions.question_text: Economics helps the government by:
options: Guiding taxation, spending, planning and stabilisation policies
questions.explanation: Economic analysis informs fiscal and monetary policy.

questions.question_text: Economics helps in understanding international issues such as:
options: Trade, exchange rates and balance of payments
questions.explanation: It explains trade patterns, tariffs and currency movements.

questions.question_text: Economics is important to a business student because it:
options: Provides understanding of markets, costs, demand and the business environment
questions.explanation: Business decisions depend on economic conditions and analysis.

questions.question_text: Which is an example of a positive economic statement?
options: India's GDP grew by 7% last year
The rich should pay higher taxes
questions.explanation: Positive statements describe facts that can be verified.

questions.question_text: Which is an example of a normative economic statement?
options: The government should provide free healthcare
questions.explanation: Normative statements express value judgements about what ought to be.

questions.question_text: The key difference between positive and normative economics is that positive economics:
options: Deals with what ought to be
Deals with what is and can be tested
questions.explanation: Positive is fact-based and testable; normative is value-based.

questions.question_text: "India's inflation was 5% last year" is a:
questions.explanation: It states a verifiable fact.

questions.question_text: "The government should provide free education" is a:
questions.explanation: It contains the word "should", expressing a value judgement.

questions.question_text: "A rise in income increases demand for normal goods" is:
questions.explanation: It states a cause-and-effect relationship that can be tested.

questions.question_text: "Petrol should be taxed more" is:
questions.explanation: It states what ought to be done.

questions.question_text: A positive statement:
options: Can be wrong if evidence does not support it, yet it is still positive
questions.explanation: Positive means testable; a false factual claim is still positive.

questions.question_text: Positive and normative economics are interdependent because:
options: Policy (normative) needs facts (positive) and facts guide choices
questions.explanation: Good policy advice requires accurate analysis of what is.

questions.question_text: The deductive method of reasoning proceeds from:
questions.explanation: It starts from general assumptions and derives specific conclusions.

tests.title: Unit 1: Introduction to Economics – Practice Test 3

questions.question_text: The inductive method proceeds from:
questions.explanation: It collects observed data and generalises from them.

questions.question_text: Which statement about the two methods is most accurate?
options: Both are complementary and are usually used together
questions.explanation: Each has strengths; theories from deduction need testing by induction.

questions.question_text: Who coined the terms micro and macro economics (1933)?
questions.explanation: Ragnar Frisch of Norway used them in 1933.

questions.question_text: Microeconomics studies:
options: Individual units such as a consumer, firm or market
questions.explanation: Examples: demand for a good, a firm's costs, price in a market.

questions.question_text: Macroeconomics studies:
options: Aggregates like national income, employment and general price level
questions.explanation: It deals with the economy as a whole.

questions.question_text: Microeconomics is called price theory because it:
options: Mainly explains how prices of goods and factors are determined
questions.explanation: Price determination is its central concern.

questions.question_text: Macroeconomics is called income and employment theory because it:
options: Explains the levels of national income and employment
questions.explanation: Its focus is determination of aggregate income, output and jobs.

questions.question_text: Which is a topic of macroeconomics?
options: Rate of inflation in the economy
questions.explanation: Inflation is an economy-wide aggregate.

questions.question_text: Macroeconomics is mostly associated with which economist and book?
options: Keynes – General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money
questions.explanation: Keynes's 1936 book founded modern macroeconomics.

questions.question_text: Partial equilibrium analysis studies:
options: One market or variable, keeping others constant
questions.explanation: Developed by Marshall; uses ceteris paribus for other markets.

questions.question_text: General equilibrium analysis studies:
options: Simultaneous equilibrium in all markets and their interdependence
questions.explanation: Associated with Walras; it considers how all markets interact.

questions.question_text: The fallacy of composition says that:
options: What is true for an individual may not be true for the whole economy
What is true for the individual is always true for the whole
questions.explanation: E.g. one person gains by saving more, but if all save more, total demand falls.

questions.question_text: The paradox of thrift states that:
options: If everybody saves more, total income and saving may fall
questions.explanation: Higher saving reduces demand and income, so total saving may not rise.

questions.question_text: Micro and macroeconomics are:
questions.explanation: Both are needed; micro behaviour sums to macro outcomes and vice versa.

questions.question_text: A limitation of microeconomics is that it:
options: Studies the individual only and cannot explain the economy as a whole
questions.explanation: Aggregating micro results can give misleading conclusions (fallacy of composition).

questions.question_text: A limitation of macroeconomics is that it:
options: May hide important differences among individual units
questions.explanation: Aggregates can conceal variations among sectors or individuals.

questions.question_text: "Price of tea in a city" is a:
questions.explanation: It concerns one product in one market.

questions.question_text: "National unemployment rate" is a:
questions.explanation: It is an economy-wide aggregate.

questions.question_text: "General price level" is a:
questions.explanation: The overall price level is an aggregate.

questions.question_text: An economic problem arises because of:
options: Scarcity of resources relative to wants
questions.explanation: Scarcity forces choice among competing uses.

questions.question_text: The three central problems of an economy are:
options: What, how and for whom to produce
questions.explanation: These choices arise from scarcity in every economy.

questions.question_text: "What to produce" involves deciding:
options: Which goods and services and in what quantities to produce
questions.explanation: E.g. wheat vs. cars, consumer vs. capital goods.

questions.question_text: "How to produce" involves the choice between:
questions.explanation: It means selecting the combination of inputs, i.e. method of production.

questions.question_text: "For whom to produce" concerns:
options: Distribution of output among members of society
questions.explanation: It depends on income distribution.

questions.question_text: The problem of full employment of resources is concerned with:
options: Using all available resources fully instead of leaving them idle
questions.explanation: Idle resources mean output is below potential.

tests.title: Unit 1: Introduction to Economics – Practice Test 4

questions.question_text: The problem of economic growth concerns:
questions.explanation: It involves how much to save and invest for future output.

questions.question_text: In a capitalist economy the central problems are solved mainly by:
questions.explanation: Prices guided by demand and supply allocate resources.

questions.question_text: In a socialist economy the central problems are solved mainly by:
questions.explanation: The state decides what, how and for whom.

questions.question_text: A mixed economy, such as India, solves the central problems through:
options: Both the market mechanism and government planning/regulation
questions.explanation: Public and private sectors coexist.

questions.question_text: Pareto efficiency is a situation where:
options: No one can be made better off without making someone else worse off
questions.explanation: It is an allocation with no costless improvement possible.

questions.question_text: Productive efficiency means:
options: Producing at the lowest possible cost using resources fully
questions.explanation: Allocative efficiency is producing the goods society wants (P = MC).

questions.question_text: Allocative efficiency is achieved when:
options: Resources are allocated to produce goods in the combination that society most values
questions.explanation: Resources are distributed according to consumer preferences.

questions.question_text: Opportunity cost is:
options: The money cost of a good
The value of the next best alternative forgone
questions.explanation: E.g. the cost of studying is the income you could have earned working.

questions.question_text: The opportunity cost of a free good is zero because:
options: It is available in unlimited quantity so using it forgoes nothing
questions.explanation: No alternative is sacrificed when a good is not scarce.

questions.question_text: Opportunity cost:
options: Can be in terms of time, goods or satisfaction forgone
questions.explanation: It is the value of the best alternative, not necessarily money.

questions.question_text: For a student, the opportunity cost of attending college includes:
options: Fees plus the earnings forgone by not working
questions.explanation: Income given up is part of the opportunity cost.

questions.question_text: A farmer can grow 100 quintals of wheat or 150 quintals of rice. The opportunity cost of 1 quintal of wheat is:
questions.explanation: 150 rice / 100 wheat = 1.5 quintals of rice per quintal of wheat.

questions.question_text: The Production Possibility Curve shows:
options: Combinations of two goods that can be produced with given resources and technology
questions.explanation: It shows maximum output combinations with full and efficient use of resources.

questions.question_text: An assumption of the PPC is:
options: More than two goods are produced
Resources and technology are given and fully employed
questions.explanation: Fixed resources, fixed technology, full employment and two goods.

questions.question_text: The PPC is concave to the origin because of:
options: Increasing opportunity cost (law of increasing costs)
questions.explanation: Resources are not equally suited to all uses, so each extra unit costs more.

questions.question_text: Marginal Rate of Transformation (MRT) is:
options: The rate at which one good must be given up to produce one more unit of another
The slope of the demand curve
questions.explanation: It equals the slope of the PPC and shows the opportunity cost.

questions.question_text: If shifting from combination A (0 X, 20 Y) to B (1 X, 18 Y), the opportunity cost of the first unit of X is:
questions.explanation: 20 − 18 = 2 units of Y forgone.

questions.question_text: A point inside the PPC indicates:
options: Unemployment or inefficient use of resources
questions.explanation: Resources are underused, so output is below its potential.

questions.question_text: A point outside the PPC indicates:
options: Unattainable output with current resources and technology
questions.explanation: It requires more resources or better technology.

questions.question_text: Which will shift the PPC outward?
questions.explanation: Growth in resources or technology expands capacity.

questions.question_text: Which will shift the PPC inward?
options: Destruction of capital in a war
questions.explanation: Loss of resources reduces productive capacity.

questions.question_text: A straight-line PPC implies:
questions.explanation: Resources are equally productive in both uses.

questions.question_text: A pivotal rotation of the PPC shows:
options: Equal change in capacity of both goods
Change in productive capacity for only one good
questions.explanation: Technology improved for only one of the two goods.

questions.question_text: Movement along the PPC differs from a shift of the PPC because movement:
options: Reallocates resources between goods with the same capacity
questions.explanation: A shift changes capacity; movement trades one good for the other.

questions.question_text: The PPC illustrates scarcity, choice and opportunity cost together because:
options: It shows the limit of output (scarcity), the choice between goods and the trade-off (opportunity cost)
questions.explanation: Limited frontier = scarcity; points on it = choice; slope = opportunity cost.
